inline.s: Above, the third [subsection] makes clear that it draws in those of lower capacities to be reborn in that land.

The bodhisattva Maitreya said to the Buddha: 'World-Honored One, in this world, how many non-retrogressing bodhisattvas will be born in that Buddha-land?' The Buddha said to Maitreya: 'In this world there are six billion seven hundred million non-retrogressing bodhisattvas who will be reborn in that land. Each of these bodhisattvas has already made offerings to countless Buddhas and shall come to be like Maitreya. The bodhisattvas of lesser practice and those who have cultivated but little merit are beyond counting, and all of them shall be reborn there. The Buddha said to Maitreya: Not only do the bodhisattvas of my land go to be reborn in that land, but the Buddha-lands of other directions are likewise. The first Buddha there is named Far-Illuminating; in his land there are eighteen billion bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn there. The second Buddha is named Precious-Store; in his land there are nine billion bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn there. The third Buddha is named Measureless Voice; in his land there are twenty-two billion bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn there. The fourth Buddha is named Nectar-Flavor; in his land there are twenty-five billion bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn there. The fifth Buddha is named Dragon-Victory; in his land there are one billion four hundred million bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn there. The sixth Buddha is named Supreme Power; in his land there are fourteen thousand bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn there. The seventh Buddha is named Lion; in his land there are five hundred bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn there. The eighth Buddha is named Free-of-Defilement Light; in his land there are eight billion bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn there. The ninth Buddha is named Chief of Virtue; in his land there are six billion bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn there. The tenth Buddha is named Wondrous-Virtue Mountain; in his land there are six billion bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn there. The eleventh Buddha is named King of Men; in his land there are one billion bodhisattvas who shall all be reborn there. The twelfth Buddha is named Supreme Flower; in his land there are countless and incalculable hosts of bodhisattvas, all non-retrogressing, wise and valiant, who have already made universal offerings to measureless Buddhas, and who within seven days can grasp the solid Dharma practiced by great ones over a hundred thousand myriad kalpas; all these bodhisattvas shall be reborn there. The thirteenth Buddha is named Fearless; in his land there are seventy-nine billion great bodhisattvas, and the lesser bodhisattvas, and bhikshus, and the like, beyond counting, all of whom shall be reborn there. The Buddha said to Maitreya: It is not only the bodhisattvas of these fourteen Buddha-lands who shall be reborn [there]. In the measureless Buddha-lands of the ten directions, those reborn there are likewise, so many and so countless. If I were to tell the names of all the Buddhas of the ten directions and of the bodhisattvas and bhikshus who are born in that land, for a kalpa of day and night I could not finish them. Now I will briefly speak of them for you.'

[Commentary] The fourth [subsection] gathers in those of superior capacities to be reborn in that land. Within it, first it makes clear that the bodhisattvas of this land go to be reborn in that land, Maitreya asking first and the Tathagata then distinguishing. From 'The Buddha said to Maitreya: Not only...' onward, it broadly shows the bodhisattvas of other lands going to be reborn there. Within that, there is first a general statement; then from 'The first [Buddha]...' it enumerates them separately. The bodhisattvas of thirteen lands go to be reborn; together with the previous Saha world, fourteen are separately enumerated. From 'Not only...' onward, it broadly raises the other lands, showing that they all go to be reborn, so many and so measureless that they cannot be fully told; this is set forth in order to make people single-mindedly seek rebirth there.
The above is the main subject.

From here on is the section on circulation [of the Dharma]. Within it there are four: first, the Tathagata praises the sutra and urges people to study it; second, from 'At that time the World-Honored One spoke this sutra...' onward, it manifests the benefit of the teaching and the awakening of the various people; third, the earth shakes and light is emitted, flowers rain down and music plays, increasing the assembly's deep faith; fourth, it shows that the benefits spoken of are broad and many, and the whole assembly rejoices together.

Within the first there are five: first, it raises the benefit of hearing and urges people to receive and practice; second, from 'I now, for the sake of all living beings...' onward, it teaches people to ask and resolve; third, from 'In the future age, when the scriptures and the Way are extinguished...' onward, it manifests the essential aiding benefit of this sutra-Dharma, that it alone remains for a hundred years; fourth, from 'The Buddha said to Maitreya...' onward, it raises the difficulty of hearing the sutra to produce in people a deeper reverence; fifth, from 'Therefore my Dharma, being thus made, thus spoken, thus taught...' onward, it concludes the exhortation to study and practice.

The Buddha said to Maitreya: 'Whoever has heard the name of that Buddha and rejoices, leaping with joy, even for a single thought, should know that this person has attained great benefit and has fully perfected immeasurable virtues. Therefore, Maitreya, even if a great fire filled the three thousand great thousand realms, one should pass beyond it to hear this sutra-Dharma, rejoicing in faith and delight, receiving and upholding, reading and chanting it, and practicing as it teaches. Why? Because there are many bodhisattvas who wish to hear this sutra and are unable to. If any living being hears this sutra, he will never retreat from the unexcelled Way. Therefore one should single-mindedly receive it in faith, and uphold, chant, speak, and practice it.'

[Commentary] Within the first there are two. First, it raises the hearing of the name of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the benefit being deep and vast, and urges [people] to study this sutra. Hearing the name relies on the sutra, and so it urges studying it. From 'If any living being hears this sutra...' onward, it shows that hearing this sutra brings vast benefit and urges people to receive and practice. In the earlier [part] showing the benefit of hearing the Buddha, 'whoever has heard the name of that Buddha and rejoices, leaping with joy, even for a single thought, has attained great benefit' shows that hearing the Buddha's name brings much benefit. From 'Therefore' onward, it urges the study of this sutra; because this sutra speaks of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, and hearing it brings great benefit, therefore even if a great fire filled the three thousand realms one must pass beyond it to hear and receive this sutra, how much more the other lesser hardships. So the following explains: many bodhisattvas wish to hear this sutra and cannot, and so one must hear it. Then in the later [part] showing the benefit of hearing the sutra, 'if one hears this sutra, he will never retreat from the unexcelled Way' raises the benefit of hearing the sutra, and 'therefore one should single-mindedly receive in faith' urges people to study and practice. Above, the first [subsection] raises the benefit of hearing and urges people to receive and practice.

'I now, for the sake of all living beings, speak this sutra-Dharma, that they may see the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and all that his land possesses. Whatever should be done, they may all seek for it. Do not, after my nirvana, give rise to doubt again.'

[Commentary] The second teaches people to ask and resolve. 'I, for living beings, speak this sutra-Dharma, that they may see the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and all that his land possesses' manifests his intention in instructing. 'Whatever should be done, they may all seek for it' is the direct exhortation to ask and resolve. From 'Do not (do so)...' onward, it wards off the doubt of later people.

'In the future age, when the scriptures and the Way are extinguished, I, with compassion and pity, shall particularly leave this sutra to remain for a hundred years. Whatever living being encounters this sutra, according to his own wish, shall all be able to attain deliverance.'

[Commentary] The third shows that this sutra, being essential, alone remains for a hundred years. 'In the future age, when the scriptures and the Way are extinguished' raises the matter of the Dharma's extinction in the future. Shakyamuni's Right Dharma lasts five hundred years, the Semblance Dharma a thousand years, and the Latter Dharma ten thousand years; when all these have passed, it is called total extinction. From 'I, with compassion...' onward, it shows his particular intention. Because the Buddha, in his compassion, pities living beings, therefore after the Dharma's extinction he alone leaves this sutra for a hundred years to ferry them over. Because this sutra reveals the Pure Land and makes people seek rebirth there, it is particularly left behind. The Great Nirvana Sutra reveals the Buddha-nature; being deep among the holy teachings, the sages first concealed it, and so it was first extinguished. This sutra teaches people to weary of suffering and seek happiness, being essential among the means of saving the common run of beings, and so it is extinguished later. The Dharma differs according to the person, and so its extinguishing differs. 'Whatever being encounters this sutra obtains his wish' shows the benefit of its remaining. After the Dharma's complete extinction, even those who hear it within the hundred years still gain benefit and are reborn in the Pure Land; how much more those who hear it now, how could any of them not be reborn? Only through the Buddha's particular intention does it show that those who now hear the sutra and seek to go there are certain to be reborn; do not be doubtful about yourself.

'The Buddha said to Maitreya: The Tathagata arising in the world is hard to encounter and hard to see. The scriptures and Way of the Buddhas are hard to obtain and hard to hear. The supreme Dharma of the bodhisattvas, the paramitas, are also hard to hear. To encounter a good spiritual friend, hear the Dharma, and be able to practice it, this too is hard. If one hears this sutra, believes and delights in it, receives and upholds it, this is the hardest among the hard; no difficulty surpasses this.'

[Commentary] The fourth raises the difficulty of hearing the sutra to produce in people a deeper reverence. 'The Tathagata arising in the world is hard to encounter and hard to see' shows the difficulty of encountering a Buddha. To be born in the Buddha's time is called 'encountering'; to see him with one's own eyes is called 'seeing'; these are both difficult. 'The scriptures and Way of the Buddhas are hard to obtain and hard to hear' shows the difficulty of hearing the Dharma. Within it, first it shows the difficulty of hearing the scriptural teachings: holding the scripture roll in hand is called 'obtaining,' and hearing it with the ear is called 'hearing'; one may also be able to receive and recite it, which is called 'obtaining,' while hearing it with the ear is called 'hearing' — all these are difficult. From 'the supreme [Dharma] of the bodhisattvas' onward, it shows that hearing their practices and Dharma is very difficult; and 'to encounter a good spiritual friend and be able to practice' shows the difficulty of practice. These above are broadly raised [as difficult]. 'If one hears this sutra, believing and delighting, receiving and upholding' is the hardest among the hard, set in contrast to the preceding three [kinds]; it shows that to study and practice within this sutra is the hardest of all. Other meanings and other Dharmas are expounded in every place, opening up the Pure Land and teaching people to be reborn there; but this one sutra alone is the hardest.
'Therefore, my Dharma, being thus made, thus spoken, thus taught, one should believe and obey and practice cultivation in accord with the Dharma.'

[Commentary] The fifth concludes the exhortation to study and practice. The word 'therefore' means: because this sutra-Dharma has many benefits, and within it study and practice are the most difficult to attain, therefore I now expound it. 'My Dharma' raises this sutra-Dharma. 'Being thus made' means: this sutra declares that Amitabha Tathagata cultivated vows and practice and obtained the body and obtained the land; this is called 'being thus made.' 'Being thus spoken' means: the Tathagata's above words expounded for the assembly; this is called 'being thus spoken.' 'Being thus taught' means: the Tathagata above taught people to be reborn [there]; this is called 'being thus taught.' This raises the preceding Dharma. 'One should believe and obey and practice cultivation in accord with the Dharma' concludes the exhortation to study and practice.
The above five sections together form the first, praising the sutra and urging study.

At that time the World-Honored One, having spoken this sutra-Dharma, countless living beings all aroused the mind of unexcelled right enlightenment. Twelve thousand nayutas of people attained the pure Dharma-eye. Two billion two hundred million devas and humans attained the fruit of anagamin. Eight hundred thousand bhikshus, their outflows exhausted, attained liberation of mind. Four billion bodhisattvas attained non-retrogression, adorning themselves with the virtue of the vast vows and, in a future age, shall attain right enlightenment.

[Commentary] Within the second section it shows the benefit of the teaching. 'Countless living beings aroused the mind of right enlightenment' raises the benefit of the vow. Having heard that Amitabha Buddha, through his vows and practice, obtained the Buddha-land and drew in and transformed living beings, they vow to be the same, which is called the mind of right enlightenment. Below, it shows the attainment of the Way, first the lesser and then the greater. The living beings of the lesser vehicle, hearing that the Saha world is foul and hateful, are deeply weary and detach themselves, and so attain the lesser fruits. Within it, first it says 'attained the pure Dharma-eye,' gaining the fruit of stream-enterer, seeing the four truthful truths, which is called the pure Dharma-eye; next comes the anagamin; and then the arhat. The living beings of the greater vehicle, hearing of the merits of Amitabha Buddha and that he broadly saves beings, firmly vow and seek, and so attain non-retrogression. Having heard of these many benefits, they vow to save beings themselves, which is called adorning the vow itself; through this they gain the fruit, and so in a future age shall attain right enlightenment.

At that time the three thousand great thousand realms shook in six ways, a great light universally illuminated the lands of the ten directions, a hundred thousand kinds of music sounded of themselves, and measureless wondrous flowers rained down in profusion.

[Commentary] Within the third section, the Tathagata's instruction having been completed, and to increase the reverence of beings, he therefore with spiritual power shakes the earth, emits light, plays music, and rains flowers. The six ways of shaking are as above.

When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the bodhisattva Maitreya and the host of bodhisattvas who came from the ten directions, the elder Ananda, the great sravakas, and the whole assembly, hearing what the Buddha had said, all without exception rejoiced.
[Commentary] Within the fourth section it shows that what was spoken benefits broadly, that the teaching harmonizes with the assemblies, and that the whole assembly rejoices together.
Commentary on the Meaning of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life, Volume Six, End.
